title: Josephus on John the Baptist and James
source_text: Ἐβουλόμην δ᾿ ἂν Κέλσῳ, προσωποποιήσαντι τὸν Ἰουδαῖον παραδεξάμενόν πως Ἰωάννην ὡς βαπτιστὴν βαπτίζοντα τὸν Ἰησοῦν, εἰπεῖν ὅτι τὸ Ἰωάννην γεγονέναι βαπτιστὴν, εἰς ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτημάτων βαπτίζοντα, ἀνέγραψέ τις τῶν μετ᾿ οὐ πολὺ τοῦ Ἰωάννου καὶ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ γεγενημένων. ἐν γὰρ τῷ ὀκτωκαιδεκάτῳ τῆς Ἰουδαϊκῆς ἀρχαιολογίας ὁ Ἰώσηπος μαρτυρεῖ τῷ Ἰωάννῃ ὡς βαπτιστῇ γεγενημένῳ καὶ καθάρσιον τοῖς βαπτισαμένοις ἐπαγγελλομένῳ. ὁ δ᾿ αὐτὸς, καίτοι γε ἀπιστῶν τῷ Ἰησοῦ ὡς Χριστῷ. ζητῶν τὴν αἰτίαν τῆς τῶν Ἱεροσολύμων πτώσεως καὶ τῆς τοῦ ναοῦ καθαιρέσεως, δέον αὐτὸν εἰπεῖν ὅτι ἡ κατὰ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἐπιβουλὴ τούτων αἰτία γέγονε τῷ λαῷ, ἐπεὶ ἀπέκτειναν τὸν προφητευόμενον Χριστόν· ὁ δὲ καὶ ὥσπερ ἄκων οὐ μακρὰν τῆς ἀληθείας γενόμενός φησι ταῦτα συμβε βηκέναι τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις κατ᾿ ἐκδίκησιν Ἰακώβου τοῦ δικαίου, ὃς ἦν ἀδελφὸς „Ἰησοῦ τοῦ λεγομένου Χριστοῦ,“ ἐπειδήπερ δικαιότατον αὐτὸν ὄντα ἀπέκτειναν. τὸν δὲ Ἰάκωβον τοῦτον ὁ Ἰησοῦ γνήσιος μαθητὴς Παῦλός φησιν ἑωρακέναι ὡς „ἀδελφὸν τοῦ κυρίου.“ οὐ τοσοῦτον διὰ τὸ πρὸς αἵματος συγγενὲς ἢ τὴν κοινὴν αὐτῶν ἀνατροφὴν ὅσον διὰ τὸ ἦθος καὶ τὸν λόγον. εἴπερ οὖν διὰ Ἰάκωβον λέγει συμβεβηκέναι τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις τὰ κατὰ τὴν ἐρήμωσιν τῆς Ἱερουσαλὴμ, πῶς οὐχὶ εὐλογώτερον διὰ Ἰησοῦν τὸν Χριστὸν τοῦτο φάσκειν γεγονέναι; οὗ τῆς θειότητος μάρτυρες αἱ τοσαῦται τῶν μεταβαλόντων ἀπὸ τῆς χύσεως τῶν κακῶν ἐκκλησίαι καὶ ἠρτημένων τοῦ δημιουργοῦ καὶ πάντ᾿ ἀναφερόντων ἐπὶ τὴν πρὸς ἐκεῖνον ἀρέσκειαν.
pass_a_gloss: I would have wished (ἐβουλόμην ἄν) to say to Celsus, having made the Jew a speaking character (προσωποποιέω) accepting (παραδέχομαι) somehow John as Baptist (βαπτιστής) baptizing Jesus, that the fact of John having been a Baptist, baptizing for forgiveness of sins (εἰς ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτημάτων), one of those who lived not long after John and Jesus recorded (ἀναγράφω). For in the eighteenth (book) of the Jewish Antiquities (Ἰουδαϊκὴ ἀρχαιολογία) Josephus witnesses (μαρτυρέω) to John as having been a Baptist and promising (ἐπαγγέλλομαι) purification (καθάρσιον) to those baptized. The same man, although not believing (ἀπιστέω) in Jesus as Christ, seeking the cause (αἰτία) of the fall (πτῶσις) of Jerusalem and the demolition (καθαίρεσις) of the temple (ναός) — it being necessary (δέον) for him to say that the plot (ἐπιβουλή) against Jesus became the cause of these things to the people (λαός), since they killed the prophesied Christ (ὁ προφητευόμενος Χριστός) — he, even as if unwilling (ἄκων), having come not far from the truth (ἀλήθεια), says these things befell (συμβαίνω) the Jews by way of vengeance (κατ᾿ ἐκδίκησιν) for James the Just (Ἰάκωβος ὁ δίκαιος), who was brother of 'Jesus the one called Christ,' since they killed him being most just (δικαιότατος). And this James Paul, the genuine disciple (γνήσιος μαθητής) of Jesus, says he saw as 'brother of the Lord (κύριος),' not so much because of kinship by blood (τὸ πρὸς αἵματος συγγενές) or their common upbringing (ἀνατροφή) as because of the character (ἦθος) and the word/teaching (λόγος). If then because of James he says the things of the desolation (ἐρήμωσις) of Jerusalem befell the Jews, how is it not more reasonable (εὐλογώτερον) to assert this happened because of Jesus the Christ? Of whose divinity (θειότης) the so many churches (ἐκκλησίαι) are witnesses, of those who have changed (μεταβάλλω) from the outpouring/flood (χύσις) of evils (κακά) and hang upon (ἀρτάομαι) the Creator (δημιουργός) and refer (ἀναφέρω) all things to pleasing (ἀρέσκεια) him.
pass_b_english: I should have liked to say to Celsus, who presents his Jew as somehow accepting John as a Baptist who baptized Jesus, that the fact that John was a Baptist, baptizing for the forgiveness of sins (Mark 1:4), was recorded by one who lived not long after John and Jesus. For in the eighteenth book of his Jewish Antiquities Josephus bears witness to John as a Baptist who promised purification to those who were baptized (Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 18.116–119). This same writer, though he did not believe in Jesus as the Christ, was looking for the cause of the fall of Jerusalem and the destruction of the temple. He ought to have said that the plot against Jesus was the cause of these things for the people, because they killed the Christ who had been foretold. Yet, as if against his will, he came not far from the truth, and says that these things befell the Jews to avenge James the Just, who was the brother of “Jesus who is called Christ,” since they killed him although he was most just.

This James is the one whom Paul, a true disciple of Jesus, says he saw, calling him “the Lord's brother” (Galatians 1:19), not so much because of kinship by blood or their shared upbringing as because of his character and his teaching. If, then, Josephus says that the desolation of Jerusalem befell the Jews because of James, is it not more reasonable to say that it happened because of Jesus the Christ? Witnesses to his divinity are the churches, so many in number, of those who have turned from the flood of evils, who cling to the Creator and refer everything to pleasing him.

choices.choice: 'Baptizing for the forgiveness of sins' echoes Mark 1:4 (also Luke 3:3); cited at Mark 1:4. Josephus' John passage is Jewish Antiquities 18.116–119 (Niese numbering; 18.5.2). The claim that Josephus blamed the fall of Jerusalem on the killing of James is not in the extant text of Josephus; Origen reports it, and it is translated as he gives it, without a Josephus locus. The quoted phrase 'Jesus who is called Christ' matches Josephus, Antiquities 20.200 (and the same words occur in Matthew 1:16 and 27:17), but here it is a quotation of Josephus, so no Scripture citation is attached. 'Josephus' is supplied in 'If, then, Josephus says' where the Greek has only 'he says', because Paul has just been named. λόγον in 'his character and his λόγος' rendered 'teaching'; 'speech' is possible. προσωποποιήσαντι rendered 'presents his Jew as' (introducing a speaking character). OCR split 'συμβε βηκέναι' read as συμβεβηκέναι. 'Flood of evils' keeps Origen's image (χύσις).
αἱ τοσαῦται ... ἐκκλησίαι: awkward 'the great number of churches bear witness, made up of' -> 'Witnesses to his divinity are the churches, so many in number, of those who'
